lines.say: Cast rings use a six thousand year old method.

lines.text: It is called lost-wax casting, because the wax model melts away.
A jeweler surrounds a wax model with a plaster-like mix.
A kiln burns the wax out, leaving a hollow mold.
Burnout can reach about 1,350 degrees Fahrenheit, or 732 Celsius.
lines.say: Burnout can reach about thirteen hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit, or seven thirty-two Celsius.

lines.text: Molten metal is pulled in by vacuum or centrifugal force.
lines.say: Molten metal is pulled in by vacuum or sen-TRIF-yuh-gul force.

lines.text: A copper amulet from Mehrgarh, in Pakistan, is about 6,000 years old.
lines.say: A copper amulet from MEHR-gahr, in Pakistan, is about six thousand years old.

lines.text: Many of the 442 objects in an Israeli hoard were lost-wax cast.
lines.say: Many of the four hundred forty-two objects in an Israeli hoard were lost-wax cast.

lines.text: Goldsmiths in the ancient Americas also cast gold this way.
Many jewelers now cast from 3D-printed patterns instead of hand-carved wax.
lines.say: Many jewelers now cast from three D printed patterns instead of hand-carved wax.

post.caption: Cast rings use a 6,000-year-old method. It is called lost-wax casting, because the wax model melts away. A jeweler surrounds a wax model with a plaster-like mix, and a kiln burns the wax out, leaving a hollow mold. Burnout can reach about 1,350 degrees Fahrenheit, or 732 Celsius. Molten metal is pulled in by vacuum or centrifugal force. A copper amulet from Mehrgarh, in Pakistan, is about 6,000 years old, and many of the 442 objects in an Israeli hoard were lost-wax cast. Goldsmiths in the ancient Americas also cast gold this way. Many jewelers now cast from 3D-printed patterns instead of hand-carved wax.
